Psychological quality of life in Brazilian medical students

Dataset 8: Resilience, learning environment and quality of life in Brazilian medical students

RSR feasibility analysis

2026-08-03

Introduction

Tempski and colleagues surveyed a random sample of 1,350 students at 22 Brazilian medical schools in 2011-2012, measuring quality of life (WHOQOL-BREF), the perceived educational environment (DREEM), resilience, depressive symptoms and anxiety in a single cross-sectional questionnaire (Tempski et al., PLOS ONE 2015; doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0131535). The psychological domain of the WHOQOL-BREF - positive and negative feelings, self-esteem, concentration, body image and meaning in life - is the domain most consistently depressed in medical trainees, and was the paper’s primary quality-of-life outcome.

Aim. Among Brazilian medical students, we examined which of sex, stage of the course, age, resilience, the perceived educational environment, state anxiety and trait anxiety are independently associated with psychological quality of life, mutually adjusting for the others.

This is a Purpose 3 analysis: several predictors are of interest and the question is which remain associated with the outcome after mutual adjustment.

Methods

Data source. Multicentre cross-sectional survey of a random sample of 1,350 students drawn from 22 medical schools across Brazil, stratified by stage of the course (basic sciences, clinical sciences, clerkship). All variables used here are complete.

Variables. The outcome is whoqol_psychological, the WHOQOL-BREF psychological domain transformed to a 0-100 scale where higher is better quality of life. Predictors are sex (reference: female, the larger group), stage of the course (reference: basic sciences, the earliest stage), age in years, the resilience scale score (16-98, higher = more resilient), the DREEM global score (sum of the five DREEM subscales, higher = a more positive perceived educational environment), and the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory state and trait scales (each 20-80, higher = more anxious). All continuous predictors are modelled per one-unit increase.

Two deliberate choices about construct overlap. First, we used dreem_global and not the five DREEM subscales, because the global score is their exact sum and putting both in one model is a perfect linear dependency. Second, we did not use any other WHOQOL domain as a predictor: physical, social and environment are subscales of the same instrument as the outcome, and a model of one domain on another describes the instrument’s internal structure rather than anything about students. State and trait anxiety are retained together because they are conceptually distinct (anxiety now versus anxiety as a disposition) and the paper treats them separately, but they correlate at r = 0.70 and their variance inflation factors are reported below.

Statistical analysis. Linear regression (lm()), justified because the outcome is continuous and roughly symmetric. We fitted a univariable model for each predictor first, then a single multivariable model containing all of them. Predictors were chosen in advance on subject-matter grounds, not by significance. Significance threshold 0.05; estimates are reported with 95% confidence intervals. Assumptions were checked with performance::check_model(). Analysis used R version 4.6.0 (2026-04-24) with tidyverse, gtsummary and performance.

Missing data. Complete-case analysis: 1350 of 1350 rows were analysed (0 dropped).

Students were young (median 22 years), slightly more often female, and roughly evenly spread across the three stages of the course. The median psychological quality-of-life score was 62.5 out of 100, well below the physical domain median in the same students, and median trait anxiety (45) was above the state anxiety median (43).

Psychological quality of life falls steeply and near-linearly as trait anxiety rises, and the three stages of the course lie almost on top of one another, suggesting the stage of the course matters little once anxiety is accounted for.

Trait anxiety is the strongest crude predictor: each one-point increase on the trait anxiety scale is associated with a 1.01-point lower WHOQOL psychological score (95% CI -1.06 to -0.96, p < 0.001). Over the observed trait-anxiety range of 20 to 80 that is roughly 61 points of the 0-100 scale, an enormous crude association. Resilience runs the other way (0.80 points per point of resilience, 95% CI 0.74 to 0.85), and the DREEM global score is positively associated with the outcome. Age and sex show no crude association, and the stage of the course shows only a small one.

Why adjustment is needed

The crude estimates cannot be read as independent effects because the psychosocial predictors are entangled with each other. Trait anxiety is a confounder of the resilience association: dispositionally anxious students score lower on the resilience scale (r = -0.61) and also report worse psychological quality of life, so part of the crude resilience effect is really trait anxiety in disguise. State anxiety plays the same role for trait anxiety - the two scales share 49% of their variance - so the crude trait coefficient absorbs situational anxiety as well. The DREEM global score is a third: students who rate their school environment poorly are both more anxious and report worse quality of life, so the crude anxiety coefficients partly reflect a bad learning environment rather than the student’s temperament. Finally age and stage of the course move together almost deterministically (clerkship students are older by construction), so any crude age effect must be read as partly a stage-of-course effect. A single model containing all seven predictors lets each estimate be interpreted holding the others fixed.

The model explains 64.6% of the variance in psychological quality of life (adjusted R-squared 0.644), which is very high for cross-sectional questionnaire data and is a warning in itself (see Discussion). Holding the other six predictors fixed, each additional point of trait anxiety is associated with a -0.58 (95% CI -0.65 to -0.51)-point change in the WHOQOL psychological score, and each point of state anxiety with -0.24 (95% CI -0.30 to -0.17). Resilience remains independently associated in the expected direction (0.31 (95% CI 0.26 to 0.37) points per point), as does the DREEM global score (0.06 (95% CI 0.04 to 0.08) points per point, so roughly 1.2 points across a 20-point difference in perceived environment). Age is associated with a small decrement (-0.25 (95% CI -0.45 to -0.06) points per year) once stage of the course is held fixed, while sex and stage of the course show no independent association. These are conditional associations in a cross-sectional survey, not effects of intervening on anxiety or resilience.

Almost every estimate shrinks toward the null, and the size of the shrinkage ranks the predictors. Trait anxiety retains the most, falling from -1.01 crude to -0.58 adjusted (57% of its crude size) - the signature of the dominant predictor in the set. Resilience keeps only 39% (0.80 to 0.31), because much of what the resilience scale captures is simply low trait anxiety. State anxiety keeps 27% (-0.86 to -0.24) for the same reason: it and trait anxiety are largely measuring one negative-affect disposition. The DREEM global score collapses hardest, from 0.282 to 0.061 per point (22% retained); its crude association was mostly a proxy for the anxiety and resilience of the student doing the rating.

Two coefficients change significance, in opposite directions. Sex is a strong crude predictor - men score 4.62 points higher, p < 0.001 - but the adjusted difference is 0.61 points and non-significant (p = 0.25): the crude male advantage in psychological quality of life is entirely explained by women in this sample scoring higher on both anxiety scales. Age moves the other way - crude -0.10 and non-significant (p = 0.47), adjusted -0.25 and significant (p = 0.011) - a suppression effect that appears once stage of the course is held fixed, because within a given stage the older students are those who entered late or are repeating. Stage of the course barely moves and stays non-significant throughout (clerkship -1.19 crude versus -0.19 adjusted).

Linearity. The fitted-versus-residual panel is flat across most of the range with a mild upward bend at the lowest fitted values: students predicted to have the worst psychological quality of life score slightly better than the model expects, because the WHOQOL scale is floored at 0.

Homoscedasticity. Breusch-Pagan rejects constant variance (p = ); residual spread narrows at high fitted values, again a scale-ceiling artefact. Because of this we refitted with heteroscedasticity-consistent (HC3) standard errors as a sensitivity check:

The robust standard errors are within a few percent of the model-based ones and no conclusion changes, so the heteroscedasticity is not consequential here.

Normality of residuals. The Q-Q plot is close to the diagonal with a short left tail; the formal test flags non-normality (p = ), but with n = 1350 this is a power artefact rather than a threat, and the central limit theorem covers the coefficient standard errors.

Influential points. No observation exceeds the Cook’s distance threshold; the largest Cook’s distance is 0.018, far below 0.5. No single student drives the results.

Collinearity. The highest VIF is 2.61 (trait anxiety), with state anxiety at 2.08. Both sit in the “moderate” band and well below the conventional threshold of 5, so the two anxiety scales can be carried in the same model - but their standard errors are roughly 1.5 times what they would be if the scales were independent, and the split of the joint anxiety effect between them should not be over-interpreted.

Discussion

Among Brazilian medical students, psychological quality of life is dominated by the student’s own affective disposition. Trait anxiety alone accounts for most of the explained variance, and state anxiety, resilience and the perceived educational environment each add a smaller independent contribution. The educational-environment association survives adjustment but is modest: a 20-point better DREEM score corresponds to about 1.2 points of WHOQOL psychological score, roughly a fifth of the effect of a 20-point difference in trait anxiety. Practically, this says that school-level improvements to the learning environment are worth pursuing but will not by themselves move a highly anxious student’s psychological wellbeing very far.

Limitations. Construct overlap is the central problem. The WHOQOL psychological domain contains items on negative feelings and self-esteem, and the trait anxiety scale contains items on the same feelings; an R-squared of 0.65 reflects partly shared item content, not only a substantive relationship. The trait-anxiety coefficient should be read as “students who describe themselves as anxious also describe themselves as having poor psychological wellbeing”, which is close to a tautology. Clustering is not modelled. Students were sampled from 22 medical schools, but the released file carries no school identifier, only school_legal_status and school_location; students within a school share teachers, curriculum and city, so the true standard errors are wider than those reported and no random intercept can be fitted. Cross-sectional design. Anxiety, resilience and quality of life were measured on the same day by the same instrument; the direction of the arrow between them cannot be established, and reverse causation (poor quality of life raising anxiety) is at least as plausible as the direction implied by the model. Common-method bias. Every variable except sex, age and the two school characteristics is self-reported on one questionnaire, so a student’s general negativity inflates all associations at once. No missing data is a genuine strength here - all 1350 rows were analysed.

Future work. A longitudinal design that measures trait anxiety at entry and quality of life a year later, with school identifiers retained so that between-school variation can be separated from between-student variation.

Feasibility notes

Not part of a student report.

  • Knits cleanly, no numerical trouble. n = 1,350 complete cases, seven predictors, no separation, no sparse cells, no influential points (max Cook’s D 0.018).
  • The real hazard is construct overlap, not collinearity. VIFs are all under 2.6, so the model is statistically stable. But trait_anxiety correlates with the outcome at r = -0.75 and bdi_depression at r = -0.74; a student who puts BDI in this model will get R-squared near 0.7 and will be, in effect, regressing one self-reported mood measure on another. bdi_depression was deliberately excluded for this reason. Students should be told explicitly that a high R-squared here is a bad sign, not a good one.
  • Do not allow other WHOQOL domains as predictors. whoqol_physical correlates 0.67 and whoqol_social 0.57 with this outcome; they are subscales of the same instrument and a model containing them is uninterpretable.
  • dreem_global and the five DREEM subscales must never appear together - the global score is their exact arithmetic sum.
  • Heteroscedasticity is flagged (BP p = ) in this and every other outcome in this dataset; it is a ceiling/floor artefact of bounded scales and HC3 robust SEs change nothing. Worth one sentence in a student report, not a re-analysis.
  • Verdict: workable, and the best-powered of the six outcomes, but only if the predictor set is policed. Left unpoliced it is the outcome most likely to produce a spuriously impressive model.
